Librogame.title: The Other and Me – The Morning Star
Librogame.author: Skarn

Changes.Change: Adapted for this app: the structure, the rules and parts of the text were changed or removed to work with its engine
Translated into English from the original French
Added sounds and background music, delivered together with the book

Librogame.ContentWarnings: Violence, fighting, a cult and its sacrificial altar. Nothing is described with complacency: the adventure is entirely in dialogue, and its tone stays that of action comedy.
Librogame.Blurb:
– Don't you think we chatter too much?
– As long as we can talk to each other, it means we're alive.
– All the same, I get the feeling all we do is talk.
– No reason the dialogue form should be reserved for cosy philosophy.
– Talk and fisticuffs?
– Talk and fisticuffs.

Page.Text:
– Remind me why I'm doing all this.
– Because you're bound to it by the pact we signed?
– Not that. This. Why am I right now strolling through the middle of a stinking sewer, sunk to my calves in a liquid whose composition I absolutely do not want to know?
– Ah, that. I sensed one of the feathers had to be around here.
– Are you sure your nose isn't blocked? Or that you're not going senile? From the very start you've insisted flat out that your feathers affect their surroundings so as to become the central element, front and centre, in plain sight, under the spotlights. And now you're telling me that actually, sometimes, they end up down the toilet by accident?
– I said the feathers always end up, sooner or later, embedded in the chest of a lich bent on world domination, in the engine of a giant robot threatening a megalopolis, and other scenarios that don't exactly shine for their restraint. However, intermediate mishaps do occur from time to time.
– Like dropping one of the most powerful objects in the world on your way to the loo?
– You leap rather quickly to whichever conclusions let you complain. If you let me explain, you'd realise its presence here obeys a certain logic.
– Since we're on the subject, if you could stop being quite so secretive and waiting until the last minute, or indeed too late, to hand me the crucial information, maybe I'd be in a better mood.
– I don't do it just to annoy you. It's simply that I jump on leads while they're still hot, and as a result the only moment I can fit the briefing in is on the job.
– Well then, go on, brief me.
– We are currently in a rough tunnel leading to the sea, dug to serve as a rubbish chute for a top-secret cutting-edge laboratory dedicated to the study of one of my feathers, and to its potential applications in the field of genetic mutation.
– Let me guess: it ended badly.
– Obviously. All that's left above our heads is a large, still-smoking crater. Which is in fact what put me on to investigating this corner.
– So, with any luck, the feather was simply carried off by their illegal sewage outflow and hasn't become the heart of some horrible chimera wallowing in a pool of acid six feet under.
– Stop being ironic and get ready to fight seriously.
– Come on, this thing can barely stand up on its eleven legs.
– Dodge its prehensile tongue instead of mocking it.
– Hey but that's ridiculous, what kind of animal has teeth on its tongue?
– The duck.
– Seriously?
– Yes.
– You're right, let's stop this lecture on the worst horrors of Mother Nature and get down to business. I'll vaporise it in no time.
– I've told you before not to use that attack at every turn.
– And every time I end up having to use it anyway once I'm backed against a wall after slogging away for half an hour for nothing. Don't you want us to cut it short this time?
– I admit I may have underestimated the danger of certain earlier situations, but…
– But?
– First, dodge that spit, as venomous as it is slimy. Second, the objections I raised in the past still stand. Not only does spending that much energy at once require drawing on my reserves, which are far from infinite, especially at this stage where I can only pull scraps out of feathers…
– But on top of that, such a deluge of power amounts to emailing our position to a whole lot of people we really don't want knowing we're here. Like for instance your ex-friend-for-life who nearly did for us last time.
– If you've learned the lesson so well, why do you refuse to apply it?
– Because if a situation like that were to happen again, I'd rather it were without the monster of the day having first made mincemeat of poor little me. It is rather easier to run away on two legs than on one.
– What do you want me to say, I can't entirely tell you you're wrong. But still, this abomination, honestly, it doesn't look all that sturdy. I think you can take it with the sword.
– Still so proud of your flaming knife, Ouro. I grant you it cuts through anything like butter, and that it's very handy for everyday nuisances… But it's not worth a good, proper disintegration.
– It's your decision. The terms of the pact only authorise me to give my opinion, not to refuse you my support.

Choice.text: I think you can take it with the sword
But it's not worth a good, proper disintegration

Page.Text:
– It's filthy, but at least it's filth produced by living beings, not dying ones.
– It isn't even filthy enough, if you want my opinion. Where are the traces of fighting? Did the crew let themselves be slaughtered without reacting?
– That's rather what I was waiting for you to explain to me.
– I have a few hundred theories in mind.
– Which is to say you have no idea.
– You've got it exactly.
– Let's see whether this helps.
– That's the third phone you've picked up; what makes you think this one will contain anything useful?
– It takes you something like five seconds to absorb the contents, there's no reason not to try.
– I'll have you know it's as unpleasant as reading a very bad encyclopaedia from cover to cover.
– And I'll have you know I'm the one taking the hits if we misjudge the threat.
– You're in luck, it's a good draw.
– What did you find?
– A lot of indigestible computer code, various entertainments, and a series of photos partly documenting life on board and its notable events.
– And so?
– And so I know who is behind all this.

– Did you know Abaddon once tried to conquer the world?
– They've all tried, several times. That one probably a bit less than the others because he isn't the most dynamic.
– Indeed. He hadn't even had the strength to invent his own plan. It was a mixture that couldn't hold together, ideas pinched from here and there, thrown against each other in the hope of a miraculous spark.
– That rings a bell. Our intelligence services had flagged a plan so preposterous that we decided to let it collapse on its own.
– You intervene in that sort of business?
– Sometimes, when our philosophy converges with the urgency of the moment.
– Your interests, you mean.
– Both at once is the ideal. And I'm beginning to see where you're going with this. The pink frills, is that it?
– The outfit isn't really what marked me. Being conscripted by force because I happened to be on the wrong street at the wrong time, before being sent off to scrap with demons on a smidgen of power, rather more so.
– I wonder how you survived that. The Orochi?
– No, no, meeting Ouro came well after. It turns out that, lazy as he is, Abaddon isn't a complete idiot. His powers are tied to dreams, and by extension to fiction. Ridiculous as the situation was, it emulated well-known narrative patterns, and, provided you played along properly, it was possible to work miracles with the crumbs of energy he'd handed us.
– So you made love and justice triumph? I thought that whole operation had been a disaster for Abaddon.
– It was. I came through it by playing on the syndrome of the episode where the heroine meets the new villain but still manages to escape without too much damage via a deus ex machina.
– The Orochi?
– Still no. I teleported.
– You can't teleport. Not on your own, at any rate. You need the level of a demon prince to work a miracle like that.
– Within the dreamer's logic, I could.
– I'll have your story checked. It is intriguing, to say the least. And it did manage to captivate me. But for all your talents as a Scheherazade, you will not live another night.

Choice.text: You will not live another night

Page.Text: A moment passes.

– I ought to feel remorse, oughtn't I?
– Why do you think that?
– Well, I'm fairly certain I broke that man's arm.
– The one who was shooting at you? I'm actually surprised you didn't smash his skull in.
– I did consider it, then I told myself that, well, it wouldn't be very nice.
– You see, you do still have remorse.
– Yes and no. I really have to make a conscious effort to remember that killing people is wrong, and to pull my punches. Whereas before, the idea would have appalled me to the core.
– I think you're idealising your past. You had never found yourself in a situation where human beings actively wanted you dead before we met.
– That's not untrue, but I still believe I've changed.
– Of course you've changed. Your organism has undergone a deep transformation. Your nervous system, your hormones, bear no relation to what you were before.
– So I'm nothing but a monster dreaming it used to be human?
– Let's say there's as much difference between your present self and your past self as between your adult self and your child self.
– What?
– Hey, puberty is no small matter.
– I suspect a bold attempt to change the subject.
– Come now, as if it were… GRENADE!
– I hate this.
– Grenades?
– No, when the situation freezes because I'm facing an imminent danger that requires a decision.
– Technically, nothing stops. On the contrary, your brain runs at full speed to perform in a fraction of a second the equivalent of several minutes' thought.
– I know. But that doesn't stop me having the extremely unpleasant impression of being a statue in a frozen world.
– Come on, you're faster than a normal human being, but not that fast. Not yet, at any rate. Your body and your senses are in the state you left them in when the thing inside your skull suddenly shifted into top gear.
– I think the fact that you can still talk to me makes the experience even more unbearable. As if every channel had been cut except the worst one.
– Don't you want to deal with this grenade instead of rambling?
– It's fine, we're not in that much of a hurry. With practice I can hold nearly five relative minutes in this state. It's not as if I have a wealth of extra options. It's too close for me to dodge. I should, however, have just enough time to disintegrate it before it goes off.
– Or else you can simply take the hit. There's likely to be some damage, but I have every confidence in your regenerative capacities.
– Your degree of confidence strikes me as heavily biased by your own interest.

Choice.text: I should, however, have just enough time to disintegrate it before…
Or else you can simply take the hit

Page.Text:
– He's rather the type to shrug off all responsibility on the pretext that there's no better school than practice. Lucky for him I catch on fast.
– You…
– Don't tell me my head's swelling. For a start it isn't true. And besides, you're very clearly on the point of collapsing. And for that to show when you already look like an old smoky ghost to begin with, you really must be at the end of your tether.
– Your…
– Your magical gibberish is a sort of virus. It forces my organism to behave in a way it shouldn't, and my brain manufactures antibodies to fight it. Bad luck for you, my brain runs very, very fast.
– That comparison is wrong on almost every level, but you've grasped the general idea.
– Oh, you're back, are you?
– I never left. His spell had merely scrambled our channels of communication, leaving you deaf and blind to my calls.
– So I was never really in danger.
– It would have grieved me to have to intervene personally for an opponent of that calibre. You are lucky, however, that he had no more time to refine his enchantment, or shaking it off would have proved considerably more delicate.
– That's a way of saying I'd have managed anyway, but that I'd have had to dig deeper into your reserves. What a skinflint you are.
– I prefer to consider myself a pragmatist who thinks in the long term.
– Don't worry, I'll pay you back right away. Give me a moment to demonstrate to this two-bit mage that the sword is mightier than the mind, and you'll be able to collect the feather's interest.

Choice.text: And you'll be able to collect the feather's interest

Page.Text:
– That was a bold manoeuvre. You exposed yourself entirely to pull it off. If I had taken so much as a fraction of a second longer to get you out, once the surprise had worn off, you'd have lost your head.
– My arms and legs were about to burn. I had to get myself out of the heart of the flames before I fell to pieces. I couldn't afford half-measures.
– I do realise that. I'm observing, not judging. And I admire your perfect timing. Did you feel me coming?
– I felt our link being forged again, yes.
– Isa must also have felt she was losing control, but she underestimated your capacity to take advantage of it.
– I have to admit I handled the distraction well.
– Indeed. She has only herself to blame, however. She only had to look at her watch instead of listening to you.
– This is where you tell me she's going to hold it seriously against me for having played her, and that she won't make the same mistake twice.
– You've got it exactly.

Choice.text: You've got it exactly

Page.Text:
– It had been a good five minutes since anyone shot at me, I was starting to think they'd grown a brain and cleared off.
– I believe a few of them did. But apparently there are at least two who have opted instead for a last stand behind a barricade improvised in the final corridor before our objective.
– We agree that at this distance, if one of the mines they've cobbled together out of elastic bands, neck warmers and their last grenades goes off, they're likely to go with it?
– Them, us, the whole floor, perhaps even their employer. They're the bravest, not the cleverest.
– I have a great urge to disintegrate all their junk. It'll be all the easier since for once it's a stationary target.
– You really must stop seeing disintegration as a universal solution to all your problems.
– As an alternative, I can try to cross this corridor of death in a few graceful bounds. But one single mistake, one single bullet ricocheting where it shouldn't, and the situation degenerates fast.
– I grant you this may be a situation where the best is the enemy of the good, and where one must know how to spend ten to avoid losing a hundred.
– One day I'll get more than a convoluted half-agreement out of you. One day.

Choice.text: I have a great urge to disintegrate all their junk
I can try to cross this corridor of death in a few graceful bounds

Page.Text:
– A brave attempt. Idiotic, but brave.
– I'd never been burcerated myself. Blimey, it hurts.
– And yet the wound is merely superficial for a being of your constitution.
– You didn't pick up on "burcerated"?
– We have made enquiries about you.
– I don't know why, but the fact that you've dug down to that level of detail scares me more than anything Ouro has told me so far.
– You are quite right to fear us.

Choice.text: You are quite right to fear us

Page.Text:
– It's still strange watching you eat a feather.
– You know perfectly well I don't really eat them, and that they aren't really feathers. Besides, you don't really see me doing it. You feel that I'm absorbing it through our link, and your brain uses that knowledge to extrapolate a mealtime scene from the orgy of colours reaching your eye.
– What I mostly notice is that you don't change one iota, when you swore to me you'd gain in presence and in power as you recovered your edible plumage.
– It's more of a stepped system. I need to reach a certain critical mass for the feathers within me to stop behaving as individual entities and to merge with each other and with me.
– That doesn't make much sense.
– I know. It's a crude approximation of physical and mathematical concepts that would take me years to explain to you properly. Rather like trying to sum up gravity as an apple falling to the ground.
– Let me put it simply: I'll believe in your famous step when I see it.
– On that subject, I have good news for you: you won't have to wait long to help me pave the way to it. I know where the next feather is.
– Already?
– In fact it's connected to the one you've just picked up. While doing my research, I discovered that the megacorporation behind that late laboratory had also got its hands on another feather, which to this day still stands as a trophy in its director's office.
– So far it sounds almost easy.
– Indeed. Following recent events, his board of directors instructed him to send that dangerous object to rot in their most remote warehouse. That didn't go down well with the little king in the three-piece suit, and, one thing leading to another…
– Yes?
– His skyscraper is now a fortress where only his personal militia moves about. He lives barricaded in his office, spending his days paying genuine worship to that sample of myself.
– What happened to him?
– Nothing but the very classic. Continuous exposure to the feather's radiance stimulated his natural paranoia and his awareness of his own age and mortality. He is now terrified at the idea of moving away from his precious regenerative charm for even a moment, convinced that death would take the opportunity to carry him off.
– How do you know all this if he's shut in?
– Walls cannot stop the reek of his fear and his pride.
– I can't get used to the idea that super-empathy is in your range of powers. It's usually a thing you associate with the good guys.
– But we are the good guys.
– It's all a question of point of view.

Choice.text: It's all a question of point of view

Page.Text:
– It hurts.
– Believe me, not as much as it should. I've patched up just the bare minimum of nerves for you to regain consciousness; most of your pain receptors are still disconnected.
– And I'm blind.
– Your eyes haven't finished repairing themselves.
– The explosion didn't miss me, did it?
– Let's say it allowed me to test the limits beyond which you can still get going again.
– Verdict?
– Luckily for you, they're very, very wide.
– And what are the guards doing while I'm convalescing?
– Oh, they put what was left of you in the beer freezer and went back to their posts.
– I can tell from your tone of voice that there's a but.
– Someone else has got hold of the feather since.
– Your family?
– I made myself very small so he wouldn't spot us, but I'm fairly sure it was one of Raguel's underlings.
– The one with the whip?
– Yes. They must have spotted us from the energy I spent saving you, and sent someone to tidy up.
– What do you want me to say… We'll do better next time.

Choice.text: We'll do better next time

Page.Text:
– You still don't know where he is, do you?
– No, sorry. His disorientation spell is deeply planted. The total absence of reaction from the crew members in the photos while their comrades vanish one by one suggests he traced it on the first day, and has done nothing but reinforce it since.
– Are we bewitched?
– The curse only affects you superficially, but yes, you're bewitched. I'm merely a collateral victim because, having no physical body, I'm obliged to use your senses as an extension of my own.
– And you can't do anything to get rid of it for me?
– In theory I could take the time to build a counter-spell. In practice it's both quicker and simpler to search the ship from end to end.
– And that won't cause me any other trouble?
– If you were an ordinary human you could wander for ever. In our case, however, the spell simply prevents us from locating him from the other end of the ship. By way of comparison, it's as if we were looking at a surveillance screen with a scrambled picture, while his victims see a doctored video.
– We know there's a problem, but we don't know exactly what.
– Precisely.
– And so?
– We'll have to go on looking for him the old-fashioned way, using your legs and your eyes.
– In short, as I was saying, you know nothing more, even if you can talk about it at length. Right. We might have more luck in the factory or the warehouse.
– If it were possible for me to forget anything at all, I'd struggle to remember we're on a ship when you put things like that.

Choice.text: We might have more luck in the factory
Or the warehouse

Page.Text:
– Do I finish him off, or…?
– That's up to you.
– But what exactly happened to him?
– I suspect the feather's radiance has been standing in for food and sleep for several weeks now.
– And when I tore it out of his fingers, he had to settle the debt retroactively?
– Oh no, not at all. It's simply that not sleeping drives you completely mad, feather or no feather. He's at the last stage of paranoid dementia now.
– I thought he'd only lost the plot this very morning?
– He crossed a threshold when he understood his drug of choice was under threat, but that doesn't mean he wasn't already a human wreck before. It's likely his underlings took so long to realise something was wrong because he was already no stranger to performance drugs.
– All the better for us. A pathetic little man is easier to handle than a monster.
– Indeed. Next time won't necessarily be so easy.

– You were quick, Orochi. But not quick enough.
– I had high hopes for this girl, Isa.
– Then you should have prepared her better for meeting me.
– Yeah. Not entirely surprisingly, I sinned through pride, I trusted my sources too much, and I underestimated my enemies' ingenuity. I really believed you were out of the game for a good while after your encounter with Gabi.
– Like every good lie, it's based on a spark of truth. It took me a month to get my sight back, and six more to recover the rest of my faculties.
– Rather good scores given the fellow's power. Tell me, weren't you interested in working for me?
– I'm over four hundred years old. Your protégées rarely survive more than a year once they're in your nets.
– A short life, but a glorious one.
– The answer is no, Orochi.
– Right, well, I'll have to find another one.

– Right, I'll have you know the thrower took to his heels when he saw you were still in one piece after taking an explosion like that head-on.
– I'm not entirely sure I really do have all my pieces.
– Enough to stand up, at any rate. What isn't strictly necessary will grow back in an hour or two.
– Glad to know that half my belly is superfluous.
– Since you no longer need to eat, it is markedly less indispensable.
– I thought you'd recycled my digestive system into weird organs linked to my new capacities?
– Yes, but nothing critical in the present situation.
– You know that one day you'll be obliged to explain all this to me in detail instead of endlessly kicking it into touch.
– It isn't so much that I don't want to explain it as that it is horribly complicated to explain. Right, shall we go?

Choice.text: Right, shall we go

Page.Text:
– Couldn't you have dropped us closer?
– I can only teleport us discreetly to nexuses I have secured beforehand. Count yourself lucky rather that I had the presence of mind to weave my web on the ice pack too, just in case.
– How would we have managed otherwise?
– I'd have arranged a more secular passage by ship. It would have taken us days to reach this corner of the world, instead of an instant and a handful of hours of bracing walking.
– Do you feel the cold?
– I can if I want to, by connecting to your senses.
– Which is to say no, since I barely find the air on the fresh side.
– Being able to adapt to extreme climatic conditions without turning a hair is one of the many advantages of your new body. Do avoid loitering in the heart of Antarctica in winter, though.
– Would it kill me?
– No. But your body would have to spend an enormous amount of energy compensating, which it would let you know about through the usual unpleasant channels. You would also be markedly more vulnerable to heavy damage in the event of an enemy attack, your regenerative capacities already saturated.
– And if that happened, could I end up as a trophy corpse studded with ice?
– If that very hypothetical situation were to occur, I hope you wouldn't run into anyone with as little taste as the author of this work of art.
– The composition is mediocre, but admit that seeing that many bodies lashed along the hull of one of these huge factory ships does have its effect.
– Let's say it's original to use a trawl net to pin humans to metal plates, industrial-spiderweb style. Quite a crowd, too. I can't swear the whole crew is there, but if not, it's not far off.
– There must still be one of them left; they didn't get themselves up there on their own.
– Perhaps.
– You've got another hypothesis in mind.
– Not yet, but I'm digging through my memories to support one. Something doesn't add up.
– In any case it won't be too hard to climb up. Even if I'd have preferred them to lower the gangway, this decorated net makes a decent ladder.
– …
– All right, now you're scaring me. You had at least fifteen ways of coming back at that with a sneer, and you didn't.
– Sorry, I was concentrating on trying to identify the source of my unease. I don't know how long it will take me to settle it or confirm it.
– And if you had to give a range?
– A few hours.
– You've accustomed me to catching on faster than that.
– Because I've usually already got past this stage by the time I make contact with you. I have in my skull several millennia of personal memories, along with access to the knowledge of every people that has walked this earth since conscious life appeared. Finding one precise piece of information from a few vague clues is like pacing a Tower-of-Babel sort of library in search of a book of which I know only the colour of the cover.
– The Tower of Babel was a library?
– It was many things before collapsing under its own lack of ambition. But that's not the point.
– To sum up: either I play it safe and wait for your ruminations to get somewhere, knowing that whoever is responsible for this display has almost certainly spotted me, because I'm as visible as an idiot standing alone in the middle of the ice…
– Or on the contrary you charge in without waiting, so as not to give him time to prepare any further for your visit, at the risk of throwing yourself into a trap laid in advance.

Choice.text: Either I play it safe and wait for your ruminations to get somewhere
Or on the contrary you charge in without waiting

Page.Text:
– Why do I feel my back is against a wall when there should be an open doorway behind me?
– My companions have raised a spiritual barrier all around our arena. The instant you crossed its threshold, neither of us could leave it any more.
– Is that what's keeping Ouro outside as well?
– You hold the Orochi in low esteem if you think that would be enough to stop him. This is merely the last line of defence of the fractal of protections isolating us from him.
– It's easy to put someone's back against a wall when you build the wall right behind them.
– Building a trap this complex was anything but easy.
– Meanwhile, I'm the one who has to fight with my arms against my body and my heels knocking against solid air, my range of movement shrunk to nothing.
– That was one of the aims.

– …
– I never much like it when you suddenly stop talking in the middle of a sentence.
– …
– And I like it even less when the silence drags on like this.
– …
– Okay. No panic. I still have the fire sword. It isn't very clear whether I can disintegrate things without the support of never-there-when-you-need-him, but let's be optimistic and assume I can. I'll also work on the basis that my regeneration still works, even if I have no desire whatsoever to check. My sense of smell is being discreet. Too discreet. And I do believe I'm losing my hearing. Yes, confirmed: I can still hear myself think, but I'm screaming in silence. Not good at all, this. At least I can still move, and therefore slaughter whoever is behind all this.
– Your courage is admirable, disciple of the Great Serpent.
– If you say so, voice in my head who is not the voice in my head I'm used to.
– The Primordial Serpent can do nothing more for you here. You are in my domain now.
– Your domain looks an awful lot like a table knocked together out of tuna tins and a mattress.
– Noble materials were lacking, but the altar is no less functional for it.
– It'll be a lot less functional once I've burcerated it.
– Burcerated?
– Burned and lacerated. Ravaged with a sword of fire, if you prefer.
– I do not believe you still have the strength to carry out even so basic a plan. From the instant you entered my territory, you became my puppet, advancing inexorably towards your destiny.
– Is your domain the whole ship or just this freezer?
– There was a time when the whole civilised world was my domain. A betrayal reduced that empire to a coffin of stone for centuries upon centuries. Recent events have made this frozen peninsula my country, this ship my capital and this cubbyhole my palace. Your blood, charged with the Serpent's power, will however allow me to move my lands somewhere more worthy of me.
– Splendid. Do tell me more.
– Do not imagine I am blind to your scheming. You are trying to buy time in the hope of finding a way out. There is none. You are wasting your last strength this very moment, struggling against me for control of your remaining senses and muscles. You are two steps from the altar, but when you reach it you will be wholly in my power, and you will lie down upon it with a smile on your lips, open to the funeral knell.
– Are you the blurry black silhouette behind the mattress?
– Blurry I am not; it is your sight that is deserting you. And that grand shadow is indeed my avatar, and in its hands rests the sacred sacrificial dagger.
– Sounds like you don't have much confidence in your ability to keep me out of action for long, if you're taking the risk of exposing yourself physically to finish the job before I get annoyed.
– Reason is leaving you along with your last strength.
– I don't think so. You know, I'm actually rather glad you cut me off from Ouro. This fight is so ridiculous that he'd have ribbed me about it for weeks. What do we look like from outside, two mimes in slow motion?
– It is entirely up to you to speed up.
– No thanks, I'd rather make you sweat. Tell me, are you struggling this much because all your strength is going into pinning me down, or is it me blocking you through the link you've woven?
– Has the Serpent taught you nothing, then?
– Ouro? Teach me things?

Choice.text: Remember one of Ouro's pieces of advice
Manage on my own
Manage on my own
Manage on my own
Manage on my own
Wait for Ouro to force his way through
Wait for Ouro to force his way through
Wait for Ouro to force his way through
Wait for Ouro to force his way through
Wait for Ouro to force his way through

Page.Text:
– A reckless counter-attack to avoid being cornered from the very first second. I appreciate the manoeuvre and its unflinching execution.
– Audacity, more audacity, always audacity, and my life will be saved.
– I wouldn't go that far. The stroke is unexpected and not entirely idiotic, but nor does it turn the game around. I am still in a dominant position.
– A chess analogy?
– I'm more of a go player.
– Good standard?
– I have a great deal of experience, but it isn't a skill I have particularly sought to sharpen over the years.
– Let me guess: you preferred to train at swordplay.
– I have learned, mastered and adapted to my needs a wide range of martial arts. Kagutsuchi is no ordinary blade, and the capacities granted by the serpent feathers make light of humanity's constraints. Sublimating them requires forging one's own way out of a multitude of experiences.
– You gave your sword a name?
– Not I. The woman who reforged it to free it from the demon's influence.
– That reminds me: what became of the other swords? The ones you took from the other girls you killed?
– You ask the right questions.
– And?
– There are secrets that must remain so.

Choice.text: There are secrets that must remain so

Page.Text:
– That's the biggest collection of frozen tuna tins I've ever seen, and I've seen a few things in my very long existence.
– They're stacked completely haphazardly, though.
– I think it's a clumsy attempt to reproduce the interior architecture of a temple of dressed stone using cardboard boxes.
– Not very impressive as temples go.
– In the religions I have in mind, ordinary worshippers didn't enter the places of worship, only the priests and the sacrifices. The decorating budget therefore went entirely on the façade.
– Human sacrifices?
– Sometimes. For a double dose of fun, I have several examples in mind where the victim had to walk up to the altar apparently of her own free will, on her own legs, so as to ease the public's conscience.
– How did they make sure she didn't ruin the ceremony by cracking at the last second and taking to her heels?
– A lot of social pressure. A little drug. And…

– I'm going to regret this so much. Be my back-up eyes, would you?
– I've told you a hundred times that I can't do that because I'm not physically present.
– Let me rephrase, purely to please you. Dear Ouro, would you be so good as to compensate for the limits of my human senses by transmitting the feather's pulses to me?
– Ah, that, of course.
– Retractable arms with retractable forearms ending in retractable claws, seriously? Isn't that telescoping a touch needlessly complex?
– Perhaps, but it's effective. You'd be dead if you were still only flesh and blood. Watch out on the left, the bit you cut off is still alive and trying to take you from behind.
– Thanks. How is that biologically possible?
– Some insects have several brains, and the feather must be giving them increased regeneration, though nothing comparable to yours.
– Doesn't stop it hurting like hell.
– Pain is a crucial warning signal. You would be far more vulnerable in combat if I took it away from you.
– That, or you're a sadist, a hypothesis I do not rule out in the slightest. Tell me instead where I have to hit this thing so it stops regrowing the bits I take off it.
– One second. Locating the feather precisely once it has merged with a living being isn't obvious, even this close. It echoes through the whole organism.
– My legs have been eaten by acid, my chest looks like Swiss cheese and the only thing stopping me screaming is that I no longer have a lower jaw, so hurry up.
– But you're still perfectly capable of expressing your annoyance through our psychic link, so things probably aren't going that badly.
– If you're waiting until I'm past complaining before you help me, it'll certainly be too late for it to do any good.
– … The feather is moving, in fact, that's why I was struggling. But it should be… To the right… Higher… There!
– Finally! But why is the other one still moving?
– It won't last long without the feather with deformities like those, but there's no reason for it to die when you take it out. It isn't a vital organ as such.
– But that's it, it can't regenerate any more?
– Indeed. You can let rip.
– Ah, that feels good.
– I can no longer tell your blood from his.
– I've just pulverised a heart bigger than my head at close quarters, that's normal.
– It's a look.
– Never mind, I'll be radiant again in a few minutes.
– Reckon on a few hours instead. Your capacity to restore yourself fully has priorities other than laundry just now.
– Can't the feather help?
– Only infinitesimally, since you'd receive a fraction of the fraction I managed to absorb from it. In other words: no.

Choice.text: The feather

Page.Text:
– That was pretty.
– And instructive. I didn't know I could disintegrate an explosion.
– Matter and energy are the same thing. It was a close-run thing, though, whether the blast was beyond the sphere you removed from existence.
– I could have taken in a larger area to be certain of making everything vanish, but it didn't seem necessary.
– It pains me to say it, but your mania for disintegrating everything in sight does at least have the advantage that you're mastering that power better and better.
– What did you think, it's all part of the plan.
– Mm-hm. In any case, after that little demonstration of your capacities, the author of that free throw doesn't seem terribly motivated to stop you any more.
– It was all calculated.
– Mm-hm again. At least the way is clear.

Choice.text: At least the way is clear

Page.Text:
– Fleur? Is that a joke about the Orochi's tendency to saddle you all with a floral pseudonym?
– Yes. I was nearly renamed Églantine, but I managed to talk him into moving on to the next name on the list.
– Euphorbia?
– No. No. The first wearable name. Fleur.
– That isn't really much less ridiculous. Just simpler. I shall never understand why a primordial entity as old as humanity lumbers its champions with names so impossible to take seriously.
– No need to look far. I think he started with a highly symbolic name like Rose, then carried on out of sheer momentum because it amused him. He can be quite childish despite his supremely venerable age.
– I earned my own name after mastering four feathers and defeating four of the serpent's chosen in single combat. You owe yours to a bad joke that refuses to die. I could almost pity you.
– Enough not to kill me?
– Enough to make an effort to be quick about it.

Choice.text: I could almost pity you
Enough to make an effort to be quick about it

Page.Text:
– Your counter-spell tickles.
– You feel it? Physically? Or is that just a joke?
– I may not have the sharpest sense of humour going, but even for me that would be a pretty rubbish joke.
– Interesting. It would seem that from playing about with my energy you have become more sensitive to power in those aspects that escape ordinary humans.
– Meaning?
– It's the equivalent of having developed an explicit sensitivity to radio waves or infrared. You consciously detect things that used to escape you entirely.
– All because I've overdone the disintegrations?
– There's no particular need to remind me, but yes. You're like a perfumer who, from working with aromas, can now pick out the subtle odours hidden behind the strongest fragrances.
– So disintegration is magic that stinks?
– There is no magic in the miraculous sense of the word. Merely energetic manipulations more or less understood by science and more or less faithfully modelled by mathematics. Disintegration stinks, to use your word, because your brain has a good grasp of its fundamental principles.
– And your magic tickles because?
– Because your brain has enough experience to know something strange is happening without being able to say exactly what. So it passes that information to you as best it can.
– I hope it isn't going to file other bits of your tinkering under nausea or worse.
– I don't want to depress you, but it's likely to happen to you at some point. I have a few thoroughly filthy powers in reserve.

– To quote him: "Complex spells are a magnificent spider's web. The best way to get out of one is to break it with a sharp blow."
– I expected better from such a teacher.
– Yeah, his advice does rather stink. Another useless one, for instance: he told me one day that there was a very simple way to neutralise any magician. All you have to do is pronounce his true name out loud and clearly. It short-circuits his spells completely, he can't do anything any more.
– A child could have told you as much. It's an elementary rule, and every worthy practitioner of the noble art begins his apprenticeship by erasing every trace of his secret name.
– You don't say, my good Ootzli Gootzli. If you'll excuse me, I'm now going to pick up my magic sword and see whether it works on a demon of smoke. Apparently, yes.
– He isn't exactly a demon. Not by the modern definition of the word, at any rate. Merely a man who gradually merged with a feather until he acquired quasi-demonic characteristics.
– Well now, you're back, are you?
– I never left. He had simply blocked the channels that let us talk. And I take back what I said: your new psychic aptitudes are not entirely useless in a combat situation.
– His brain was a bit of a labyrinth, but since you'd told me his life story it wasn't too hard to work out the layout and find which corner he'd stashed his name in.
– All the same, that's fine work.
– It was easy, I have plenty of experience with manipulative demons.
– Finish him instead of joking.
– It's fine; men like that, once their machiavellian plans are in pieces, are good for nothing.
– Please don't you fall into the cliché of smugness as well.
– And this from the divine one with the ego… It's funny, every time he loses a piece he contracts to get his starting shape back, only smaller.
– At this stage he's no more than a barely conscious mass of energy around a feather. The more matter you remove, the more what's left clings to the centre of gravity; that's normal.
– For a certain definition of normal.
– All of which is to say: keep digging, and one more feather…
– … Will fall into my hands.

Choice.text: Will fall into my hands

Page.Text:
– Tell me.
– You know some of my feathers have been out in the world for a very long time.
– You're not going to tell me the story of your fall again?
– No, I'm talking about more recent events than that. Nothing going back more than five thousand years. At that time one of my feathers had fallen into the hands of a rather clever fellow who had also had the luck to observe personally the harmful side effects of a rapid, uncontrolled absorption of that power.
– Clever enough to take his time, not wise enough to throw it straight into the ocean?
– You've got it exactly. He experimented for years, learned to master some of its properties, until he became a powerful thaumaturge. At that stage he did what every sufficiently powerful sorcerer does: seize the throne.
– And he reigned until the inevitable betrayal that sealed his fall.
– Exactly. After long years of absolute power during which he completed his fusion with the feather, he was defeated by cunning, shut in a stone sarcophagus covered with inscriptions saying who he was and that he must never, ever be freed…
– In a language nobody speaks any more today. Not that it would have changed anything if it had been comprehensible. Who listens to warnings like that?
– His contemporaries were no doubt counting above all on the fact that this cumbersome parcel would never come back up from the ocean floor where they had thrown it. But, with the evolution of technology, it was eventually fished out.
– And obviously they couldn't just have done him in.
– Clever sorcerers begin by making themselves invulnerable to conventional weapons and to poison. Then to hunger, to lack of oxygen, and so on.
– Tell me he isn't immune to flaming swords and disintegration.
– Of course not. I designed those weapons precisely to remind such nuisances of their mortality.
– So, in your view, they fished out a more-than-ancient sorcerer who woke up in a foul mood. But from there to killing everyone?
– Oh, he was already practising mass sacrifice before his stay in the water. I imagine his thoughts weren't very clear after several millennia of coma, and that only once fully sated with vital energy did he realise there was nobody left to serve him.
– The equivalent of a small town as a snack?
– There's a reason king-sorcerers rarely reign more than a handful of years. When a human being suffers a small annoyance, even someone usually very level-headed, they sometimes break a small object. When a magical monarch is in a bad mood, even one who is normally a rather enlightened and respected overlord, well, he sometimes breaks a city and all its inhabitants.
– And did that one often have bad days?
– Yes, from what I've read he was rather a bad-tempered, unpleasant sort.
– Right, now that we're not in much doubt about him being a villain, shall we kill him?
– Of course.

– That was impressive. Nicely handled, your brain's higher gear.
– Failing to predict the ricochets, it gave me the time I needed to act accordingly.
– I feared the worst when that bullet passed a hair's breadth from the grenade, but you managed to parry it at the last moment.
– I'd have preferred to parry it earlier, if I'd been physically capable of it.
– Soon, soon. Once we've recovered enough feathers. In the meantime I have the distinct impression that you're getting better and better at handling your inhuman capacities, which bodes well for what follows.
– Your compliments have a sinister ring. As if you were preparing me morally for the next stage of my irreversible transformation into an infernal abomination.
– I speak from experience when I tell you that most chthonic creatures are more pleasant to look at than what awaits us behind that door.

Choice.text: I speak from experience when I tell you that most chthonic creatures…

Page.Text:
– And ridiculous control spells.
– Ridiculous how?
– Like trying to steer a charging rhinoceros by sticking a few strings on it.
– And what happens to the comic-opera puppeteer in your story?
– He tries to flee when he realises the rhinoceros has no intention of stopping or changing direction.
– Is he faster than a rhinoceros?
– No, as he eventually realises. So he tries to hide.
– And does that work?
– No, because the strings have stayed stuck to his fingers, tracing a clearly visible trail to him.
– Do you wish to describe what happens when the rhinoceros finally catches up with this puppeteer who was far less clever than he thought?
– I shall leave that scene to the audience's imagination. Let's simply say it's brutal, quick, and that once the job is done nothing remains but a shining feather.

Choice.text: Quick, and that once the job is done nothing remains but a shining feather

Page.Text:
– Is that blood on the floor?
– Yes and no. There is blood in the heap, but fish blood. It's waste from the catch left there to rot.
– Is there no way to switch off my sense of smell?
– I can dampen it considerably without difficulty. Is that better?
– Much better, thanks. I can finally concentrate on something else. Like finding whoever is responsible for this mess.
– Easier said than done. The deck is deserted. And the ship is enormous.
– If only one of us supposedly had the power to detect feathers.
– My senses are being scrambled by something aboard this ship, and believe me, it's about as pleasant as if you couldn't hear anything because a cloud of bees was buzzing in your ears.
– Fine. What can you tell me about this ship?
– That this behemoth comes down to four large sections: the fishing and navigation part, which you're looking at now. The factory part, which turns fresh fish into tins. An enormous refrigerated, compartmented hold to store those tins. And a real little village to house all the people needed to produce them.

Choice.text: The factory part, which turns fresh fish into tins
An enormous refrigerated, compartmented hold to store those tins
And a real little village

Page.Text:
– I'm impressed. You managed to bend the kekkai for a few moments, just enough to dodge my attack and break free.
– Fear of death is an excellent motivator.
– And mastery of matter through thought a talent I didn't know you could exploit without the Orochi's help.
– Believe me, if I really had access to my disintegration, you wouldn't be this smug.
– Oh, I'm perfectly aware of that. During one of my earlier fights, we had only imperfectly separated your protector from his champion of the time. Half my body turned to dust in an instant.
– You survived a disintegration?
– A partial one. Luckily for me, she drew that ultimate weapon a moment too late. My companions managed to finish her off and save me.
– This is where I regret that Ouro doesn't have a whole team backing him up.
– According to some sources he has tried to assemble one on several occasions.
– What went wrong?
– Claim the contrary as he may, the Orochi is extremely bad at understanding and cooperating with humans.
– And me? And the other girls before?
– That's what I'm saying. He has to carry out a meticulous selection, followed by a deep physical transformation, in order to manage to act in harmony with a person.
– It's true he isn't easy to live with day to day, even though we communicate mind to mind with no possible misunderstanding. Unless we do it on purpose for the joke, of course.
– I'm convinced that a certain compatibility of senses of humour is among his criteria.

Choice.text: I'm convinced that a certain compatibility of senses of humour is…

Page.Text:
– Back again for a new adventure.
– One that smells like a leaky pipe.
– Meaning?
– In theory it's an easy feather. It's in stasis, which means its power isn't accessible to the common run of mortals.
– Is that possible?
– Complicated, but possible. It amounts to using the feather as the battery of a force field that isolates it from the outside world. Apart from you, me and the usual big shots, there aren't many people capable of breaking a shell like that.
– What's the point of the manoeuvre?
– To take a feather out of the great game, at least temporarily. In the case that interests us, it was the driving force behind half a century of war between five feudal lordships, changing sides after each defeat or victory without any party keeping it long enough to really exploit its power.
– How did it end? Did a pacifist hero come from afar to steal the feather and seal it in a sanctuary deep in the mountains? Or was one of the belligerents simply a bad loser who decided that if he couldn't have it, nobody would?
– It depends who's telling the story. In any case the feather ended up as a decorative ornament far from prying eyes, mine included, for long years. But you know how it is with feathers: they never stay hidden for ever.
– Fortunately, otherwise my servitude would be eternal too.
– Certain minor demons don't hesitate to have people sign contracts as rotten as that, but I'm above all that.
– Sure you are, I'll just… Why have I shifted into that state where I feel time has stopped?
– Because you're in mortal danger.

Choice.text: Because you're in mortal danger

Page.Text:
– You didn't already know?
– Let's say I've moved from an informed hypothesis to absolute certainty.
– Does that change anything in practice?
– Yes and no. The confirmation itself is incidental, but by cross-referencing my knowledge of the subject with the photographic traces, I'm able to guess how our man occupied his days until the last witness vanished.
– Not weaving flower crowns to welcome us, I assume.
– No. Building himself, metre by metre, a sanctuary, an enchanted zone in which people disappeared discreetly, leaving the other crew members only a confused memory of their existence.
– What exactly did you work that out from?
– From a pile of small details, but the photo where a man is having his throat cut in the shadows in the background while nobody in the foreground seems bothered did help a lot.
– Let me guess: he has extended his zone of influence to the whole ship and is watching us this very moment.
– I even think he's been watching us since I materialised us on the ice. He is, however, far from powerful enough to affect us outside the heart of his domain. Which ought to be, if I go by the location of his first attacks, at the far end of the refrigerated hold.
– The converse of your previous statement: do I risk anything going down there with one hand on my heart and the other on the hilt of my sword?
– Hard to say. A being's power isn't easily quantified. I wouldn't venture more than an estimate of yours, and I'm with you daily, so a man I have only indirect testimony about — a mystery.
– That's hardly reassuring.
– I'm not reassured myself. Much as it grieves me, it might be more prudent to spend a little of my accumulated energy to reinforce your mystic defences temporarily. I have enough information to weave adequate protective enchantments at lower cost.
– Better quality than what you offered me outside?
– No, similar. No point stacking the two, it would be a waste of energy.

Choice.text: At the far end of the refrigerated hold
Accept the mystic reinforcement
Ask him how it works

Page.Text:
– Since we were no longer counting the minutes, I also took the opportunity to refresh my memory on a number of counter-spells that should reduce his magic to a spring breeze.
– I assume there's a "but", otherwise you'd have told me you'd already cast the lot, not that you could.
– My information is imperfect, which obliges me to aim broadly if I want to cover every case. In other words, to draw on my reserves to reach a satisfactory result.
– Are you asking me to choose between carrying out this mission in the great cold in the least impressive way possible, or keeping the option of disintegrating one more thing later on?
– Let me rephrase so this decision demands some thought from you: accept a calculated loss of energy here to avoid a possible greater loss of energy later, and therefore perhaps maximise the number of disintegrations in the long run.
– Ah, yes, now that's a real choice.

Choice.text: In the least impressive way possible
Keeping the option of disintegrating one more thing

Page.Text:
– Are you getting anywhere? It's been about three hours now.
– Do you realise that in that fleeting span I have managed to cross-reference the history of the ocean currents, the entire literature on enchantments based on macabre circles of corpses, and the esoteric history of a quarter of a hemisphere over more than ten thousand years?
– No, I don't realise. And I don't care. Did you find something?
– Oh yes. I know exactly who is waiting for us.

Choice.text: I know exactly who is waiting for us

Page.Text: The space of a breath.

– I feel like I'm walking through the set of a horror film.
– Then again, you're walking past machines designed to shred several tonnes of flesh an hour, twenty-four hours a day. Count yourself lucky they're stopped and that you aren't strapped to the conveyor belt.
– Don't give our villain of the day ideas.
– Don't pretend that wasn't exactly the first thing you thought of when you got here.
– Of course it was. That's why I slammed the emergency stop, just in case.
– And cut the power supply cables into the bargain.
– You never know.
– As a result, here we are in the dark with only the emergency lights.
– Not that it's much of a problem, given you've tinkered with my eyes so I can see perfectly anyway.
– You almost make me nostalgic for the beginning of our adventures, when you marvelled at the slightest little thing.
– If I'd stayed that girl, I'd be nothing but dust today.
– I know. I'm a doting father complaining that his offspring isn't as sweet as she used to be, while actually rather glad not to have to change her nappies any more.
– Awkward comparison aside, this place is empty as empty gets.
– Yes. Despite the perfect setting for a fight for the ages, it's a bad draw.
– That leaves the crew quarters or the storage hold.

Choice.text: That leaves the crew quarters
Or the storage hold

Page.Text:
– Unsurprisingly, an explosive that no longer exists can no longer explode.
– And I didn't even have to shake them to make them clear the way. All that's left is to go through the door.
– Then again, in their position you'd be just as rattled. They watched all the junk they'd covered the corridor with vanish into thin air.
– Please don't remind me that we sometimes run into people with this kind of power on the other side, or I'll give us both depression.
– If you keep using it this often, you'll soon be as strong as they are at this little game. And I'll be an emptied wineskin.
– In any case, it isn't your passive-aggressive compliments that are going to convince me to stop.

– Will you not die, then? You are no more than a charred skeleton and yet you keep slipping away from my blade.
– There's no mirror to hand, but I'm convinced your description is slightly exaggerated. I couldn't still move if my muscles were ashes.
– Of course you could! By using the Orochi's energy to compensate for your physical absences.
– Oh? I knew it was technically possible, I was hoping I'd managed to develop my capacities far enough to do it, but I really wasn't sure of my ground. Nice of you to confirm it, though I'd have preferred it in other circumstances.
– Are you mocking me?
– Less than you think. I'm not this extreme when I train.
– That is a mistake.
– I'd rather not die in training so as to shine in the field. Besides, I need this in order to be brilliant, as you can see.
– I confess we underestimated you and the Orochi. He will be back at any moment, and we do not have the firepower immediately available to eliminate you before then. We shall not make that mistake twice.
– Then you won't hold it against me if I spend the last moments before Ouro takes me away from here wishing we never meet again.

Choice.text: Then you won't hold it against me if I spend the last moments before Ouro…

Page.Text:
– That bad?
– Oh yes. Describe what you see to me.
– An underground car park. Far too empty even at this hour of the night.
– Yes, supposedly we should have found a lorry full of cheap antiques there with the feather hidden among them. Now stop joking, and describe what is right in front of your eyes.
– All right, I'm just trying to lighten the mood. I assume the danger comes from the silhouette in modern military armour in a combat stance holding what looks horribly like my fire sword.
– That's normal, it's virtually the same one bar the forging flaws. The additions you see are merely there to cut it off entirely from my control.
– You can control my sword?
– I can only modulate the intensity of the flame or make it self-destruct. Precisely to avoid a stroke like this one. But I missed the timing back then.
– A former apprentice of yours who found a loophole in the contract and holds a bit of a grudge?
– From a certain point of view. And by that I mean death is a valid escape clause and that she probably holds it against me that she was disarmed and killed by her own weapon while I watched, powerless.
– What happened?
– I sinned through pride.
– I'll hold back all the easy jokes I could make, because I can see her moving imperceptibly, which means either that your killer is extremely fast or that my suspended time is reaching its limits.
– A bit of both. And killer in the feminine, technically. Her war name is far too pretentious for my taste, so I just call her Isa.
– You do know how to make yourself liked.
– Always. About four hundred years ago I fell into a trap. I'm generally rather good at avoiding them, but I also have a great many enemies, so statistically I'm bound to slip up now and then. That attempt was particular in that, though it wasn't exactly the first time, it was humans trying to catch me, and not the usual cranks from either camp.
– Get to the point, please.
– The context is unfortunately important. I could probably have got out of it if I hadn't completely underestimated their capacities. But I had remained relatively sealed off from the latest technological developments, in every field, and was caught entirely off guard by an ingenious seal completed in an instant by a few well-placed explosives. I lost contact with my protégée of the time, and never found it again.
– Because she'd been killed in the meantime.
– Yes. By cross-referencing, I eventually discovered she had been overwhelmed by a simultaneous assault during which someone managed to tear her weapon from her. Without my direct support, she didn't survive being beheaded by a flaming blade.
– I see. So you're warning me that I'm likely to be burcerated very soon, and in a wholly fatal way in your absence.
– Yes. No disintegration, no teleportation, limited regeneration. Don't even try to beat her. Buy time until I come back and can get you out. Make her talk if you can. She loves the sound of her own voice.
– If you know her personally when she's responsible for an incident four centuries old…
– I'm not sure she was the brains or the arm behind the first murder, but she's the one who has had the sword since, and she has personally assassinated several others. Oh, and she's bound in a fairly complex way to at least three feathers, which makes her more or less immortal.
– Joy.
– Make the most of the advantage you have of being able to choose your approach to the problem calmly. It may be your last action if you get it wrong.
– I understand perfectly. Fundamentally, since she's very clearly trying to behead me in a single stroke, and I'm already too close to dodge entirely, I have only two options: parry by the defensive book, taking a step back or on the contrary block her blade out in front of my body to bring the fight to her.
– Remind me to arrange proper fencing lessons for you if by some miracle we get out of this. And…
– Yes?
– Good luck.

Choice.text: Taking a step back
Or on the contrary block her blade out in front of my body to bring the…

Page.Text:
– Isa? Isa? The Orochi told you my name was Isa?
– Er, yes?

That he should hand over that knowledge so easily, and reduce so prestigious a name to so banal a diminutive, merely underlines his infinite contempt.
– He's made of pride, you know. I really think he's physically incapable of treating anyone without condescension.
– One might think he would learn, for all the times he has burnt his wings on the flame of his own arrogance.
– I'm not sure beings like him are capable of evolving. They give me the impression of actors imprisoned in their role.
– You have known others besides the Orochi?
– I've had an eventful life.

– I don't really know. I don't much want to talk about it. But at the same time, maybe I should.

Choice.text: I don't much want to talk about it
But at the same time, maybe I should

Page.Text:
– You know, Ouro, as much as I hate everything you drag me into, I have to admit that this power here absolutely rocks.
– Oh, I think I can understand, intellectually at least, the fascination that the capacity to annihilate matter at a level so fundamental that it becomes pure light can exert on a purely physical being. I am merely convinced that your immoderate love of disintegration does not make you an impartial judge of whether to resort to it.
– Don't be a killjoy, just admire. No more monster, and your feather floating peacefully in the middle of nothing, intact, waiting only to be picked up.
– Technically, it was destroyed for a fraction of an instant before recomposing itself identically from its diffuse energy and its residual memory.
– Does something that took place over a time interval so small that no technology on this planet, and to a lesser extent my senses, is capable of grasping it really matter to our business?
– Do you really want to embark on a philosophical debate on the subject?
– No.
– Then let me mourn reserves patiently accumulated year after year and emptied in a moment so short you refuse even to conceive of it.
– Come on, stop grumbling, you know perfectly well you'll get back straight away, through the feather, part of what you've just spent, and that it will give you far more in the long run.

Choice.text: You know perfectly well you'll get back straight away, through the feather

Page.Text:
– Hey, I thought we were going for an honourable one-on-one duel!
– Time is running out.
– I can well believe Ouro will turn up at any second, but flamethrowers? Seriously?
– Be quiet and stay where the beams cross.
– What next? And you're burning too, I'll have you know.
– If I break out of our clinch, you'll be able to run.
– And it doesn't bother you that much to end up as a melted candle?
– I shall survive. My outfit is partly fireproof and the feathers' power will heal the burns within a few weeks at worst.
– And your warrior's honour?
– I think you have the wrong film. It was never a question of honour, merely of pragmatism. Had I been in a position to dispose of you within the deadline by the sword, we should have made substantial savings in materials and time. Be proud rather of having pushed me into a corner.

Page.Text: A second, barely.

– Okay. And by the way, how do you manage to talk inside my head?
– The channel that normally links you to the Orochi is now plugged into me.
– That line isn't only for talking, you know.
– At present it is. Our undesirable mutual acquaintance blocked all the other channels as a matter of urgency just before his enforced visit to the infernal realms. He was no doubt afraid I might find a way of using them against you.
– Oh, would you by any chance already have defeated another girl that way?
– He really does train you all as badly as ever. The answer is yes, of course, and the details are a secret I keep to myself.
– Go on, don't be coy, tell me.
– What would be the point? Your extraordinary physical capacities do not entirely make up for your total lack of technique. You are doomed to leave me an opening at any moment, and to pay for that mistake with your life.
– Is this second step compulsory? Can't we just sit down and talk?
– Oh, I have nothing against you personally. You merely have the misfortune of being the puppet the demon needs in order to interact with the physical world. Your demise means years, perhaps even decades, in which he won't be under our feet, the time it takes him to find and raise a replacement.
– If I promise not to help him any more, that's completely implausible, isn't it?
– Given that your pact compels you to do exactly that, indeed it is.
– Come on, Isa, I'm sure you can do a Fleur a favour.

Choice.text: Come on, Isa
I'm sure you can do a Fleur a favour

Page.Text:
– Well rested?
– Frankly no. Knowing you could reappear at any moment to send me off on some new urgent mission ruined all my free time. The more the days passed, the more I felt something terrible was about to land on my nose and that I had to be ready to leave at any moment.
– Yes, I gathered you were fairly stressed. I even had the impression you were training.
– As far as possible. I don't need cardio or weights with this body, and since you won't tell me anything, I have no idea how to develop my new capacities effectively.
– Because I know nothing about it. The pact affects each person differently. And I have no idea how to teach you skills that are as instinctive to me as breathing.
– Do I still breathe?
– Yes, although what you exchange with the atmosphere is no longer exactly oxygen and carbon dioxide. But we're getting off the subject. I have a new lead.
– When you start like that instead of announcing that you know where a feather is, it means you aren't sure of your ground at all, and there's a nine-in-ten chance I'll be making a round trip for nothing.
– You know me well. Indeed, this time I have only circumstantial clues. A trawler ran aground on the polar ice, and has not responded since. The last radio messages received are confused, but hint that the situation gradually spiralled out of control following a thoroughly illegal catch that scraped the seabed and brought up debris along with the fish.
– The connection with your plumage isn't leaping out at me.
– Tying one of my feathers to a large rock and throwing the lot into the water is a simple but apparently effective method of getting rid of one of my feathers.
– Apparently?
– They always come back up through improbable coincidences. Or rather, improbable only for those who do the sums leaving their influence out of the calculations.
– That's even worse than I thought. You really have nothing more than a suspicion based on an anecdote that could be explained in plenty of other ways?
– Would you rather not go and check, let the ship sink, let the feather that may be aboard go back to spending a few more decades or centuries at the bottom of the ocean, during which time you will remain at my disposal because you undertook to back me up until I had recovered all my feathers?
– When you put it like that, I'm suddenly more motivated. What are we waiting for?

Choice.text: What are we waiting for

Page.Text:
– It's a nice story, this four-times-four. Shame it's completely false.
– What? What are you talking about?
– Your little group? Order? Organisation? Anyway, you and those other men did indeed manage to get hold of four feathers, five counting the one you used to bait us. But you aren't capable of really using more than two at a time.
– But how…?
– And you've killed three champions with your own hands at a generous count, one if you leave out the ones where you had a great deal of help.
– You…
– And your great friends circling around us right now knew nothing about any of it, because the advantage of being four hundred years old is that there aren't many witnesses left to contradict you, and your little internal propaganda has every interest in putting you on a pedestal.
– 臭婊子! You're a minor telepath. You can read my surface thoughts. You're merely repeating what comes into my mind.
– You shouldn't have been such a bad liar. When you tried to bluff me, your brain practically screamed the truth inside my skull.
– I knew the Orochi had that sort of power, not that you had inherited it.
– I think it exists in a dormant state in the party bag he hands all of us when we sign the pact, but that the other girls generally prefer to develop skills that are more directly useful in combat.
– And they're quite right. What possessed you to push in that direction?
– I like varying my strategies, and therefore having a wide range of skills.
– Usually, taking your heads off brings me nothing but the satisfaction of a job done, but this time I shall do it with undisguised pleasure.
– Come and take it.

Choice.text: Come and take it

Page.Text:
– Mad to think that while he's basically dying of brutal withdrawal, it's still the value of his shares that obsesses him.
– How do you…? Oh, you've picked up that power too.
– Wasn't that planned?
– With experience, and the strengthening of our link through obtaining new feathers, you were going to develop new capacities sooner or later. But I expected them to be more martial.
– Hey, I like variety. What's frustrating is that it doesn't seem to work on you.
– What will really frustrate you is when you realise it doesn't work on the big fish on the other side either. Generally speaking, it's an incidental skill. I'm not even sure what use it will be to you later on.

Choice.text: I'm not even sure what use it will be to you later on

Page.Text:
– Bad experience?
– Are there good experiences with demons?
– There are plenty of legends where the demon gets taken for a ride.
– Yes, I never quite understood the moral of those stories. Is it all right to manipulate and humiliate people if they're wicked and manipulative themselves?
– Morality is a complex and changeable thing. I must inform you, however, that in the present case I don't know whether I'm the good one, but I certainly don't intend to let you manipulate me any longer.

Choice.text: But I certainly don't intend to let you manipulate me any longer

Page.Text:
– Ah, about time!
– It's fine. I had to break the banishment enchantment by brute force, and you know how costly that is for me.
– Yes, I know. Which is precisely why I'm usually the one who carries out all these menial tasks that require interacting directly with the physical world.
– And so?
– And so what? You're the specialist in all these magical contraptions. If even you got caught out like a rookie, don't go lecturing me afterwards.
– I grant you I did not shine. I probably underestimated that pathetic little man too badly.
– Don't worry, it isn't as if he'll still be in a fit state to testify after what I'm giving him.
– My reputation matters little to me. I'm rather more worried about what will happen to us the next time we run into someone genuinely dangerous, if I'm already fumbling against a second-rater.
– Console yourself: at least you'll have one more feather for that hypothetical future encounter, which I'd be glad to put off as long as possible.
– You're right, let's refocus on what really matters.

Choice.text: Console yourself: at least you'll have one more feather

Page.Text:
– Ouro, we're going to have to review our strategy. I'm risking my life a bit too much lately.
– How shall I put it… Would you prefer a comfortable illusion or the truth?
– Go for the truth.
– At the start of our collaboration I deliberately favoured the leads that carried the least risk, just to give you time to adapt. Nearly dying every time is in fact considerably closer to the norm in this line of work.
– Hold on, that sort of nightmare monster last month that vaporised half my body with a look, and I don't even know how I managed to regenerate afterwards — that was supposed to be easy?
– Barachiel? No, that one was a miscalculation. And you didn't manage it: I recreated the lost pieces from scratch with my own energy. Good reflex, though, to have kept running even with part of your chest and one arm missing.
– Flattery will get you nowhere today. You promised me then that by keeping a low profile it wouldn't happen again.
– Knowing me, I must have phrased that more ambiguously.
– Obviously. And knowing you, I didn't believe it anyway.
– Understandable, even though I was entirely serious. I really thought I could carry on zigzagging between the real troubles a while longer if I chose my interventions carefully.
– But?
– I can't foresee everything. Fortunately, incidentally, because prescience really is a rotten power, one of the worst possible curses.
– You'll get away with a digression this time, Lux Ferre.
– Straight out with the grand names, you really are furious. Yes, I got it wrong. I underestimated every camp, I thought they'd take longer to adapt to my return and your arrival, and it nearly went badly wrong.
– And so?
– And so we're going to step up the pace.
– What?
– This isn't a game where we can afford to be cautious. If people like Isa are starting to be able to predict our moves, it means we're at most two moves ahead of Michou. And believe me, you don't want to run into Michou before we've got our hands on another good twenty feathers.
– How dangerous is he?
– He's the one who tore my wings off at the beginning of time. Since that original incident, he has returned more of my protégées to dust than all the other threats put together.
– And so your magnificent plan for avoiding my certain death is?
– To make gambits worth the risk, rather than risking losing everything for a single feather.
– Meaning?
– Meaning we're going to pay my family a visit.
– Which side?
– Hey, I intend to play for high stakes, not to send you to the slaughter for nothing. So we'll stay within a minimum of reason, and content ourselves with a trip to Hell.
